title: Phrasal Verbs
goal: Use the phrasal verbs that native speakers actually reach for, and know when not to.

I ran into her. (not ran her into)
I can't put up with it.
Call it off is spoken. Cancel it is written.

phrases.use: Note the -ing after to. Looking forward to see is the classic error.

phrases.use: Postpone, in speech. In an email you would write postpone.

phrases.use: The pronoun must go in the middle. Turn down it is wrong.
Softer and vaguer than it failed, which is why people use it.

phrases.use: Look after is inseparable. Look it after is wrong.

reading.title: Why phrasal verbs are hard, and why you still need them
reading.text:
Almost every phrasal verb has a single-word equivalent, usually with Latin roots, and Portuguese speakers already know most of those words: postpone, tolerate, discover, cancel, investigate. This produces a tempting shortcut. Why learn "put off" when "postpone" exists and is, if anything, clearer?

The answer is register. A speaker who only uses the Latinate word sounds like a document. "I cannot tolerate this noise" is correct, and no colleague has ever said it out loud. "I can't put up with this noise" is what the sentence sounds like in a kitchen at work. The reverse mistake exists too: an email that says "we had to call the whole thing off" reads as careless where "cancelled" would have read as professional. Neither register is better. They are two different rooms, and fluency is largely knowing which room you are standing in.

The grammar is the smaller problem, but it does have to be learned rather than guessed. Separable verbs push a pronoun into the middle: turn it down, never turn down it. Inseparable ones refuse to be split at all: I ran into her, never I ran her into. Three-part verbs behave as a single frozen block. There is no rule that predicts which is which, and pretending otherwise wastes time. Learn each phrasal verb with a full example sentence attached, and the pattern comes along free, in the only form you will ever need it.

questions.q: What is the writer's main point about phrasal verbs?
options: They belong to a different register than their Latinate equivalents
They are always better than single words
They should be avoided in speech

questions.q: Why does "I cannot tolerate this noise" sound wrong to a colleague?
options: It is too formal for spoken English

questions.q: What does the writer say about the reverse mistake?
options: Phrasal verbs in a written email can read as careless
It is worse than the first mistake

questions.q: What advice does the writer give for learning them?
options: Learn each one with a full example sentence

questions.q: "Fluency is largely knowing which room you are standing in" is a metaphor for ___.

speaking.tip: Four words, one wave. Forward to blends into forward-tuh.

speaking.text: I can't put up with it any longer.
speaking.tip: Put up with is three unstressed beats. Longer carries the weight.

speaking.text: The car broke down on the motorway.
speaking.tip: Broke DOWN. In a phrasal verb the particle usually takes the stress.
Turn it links into turn-it. Down is the loud part.
Work OUT, and the final t is barely there.

speaking.text: I came across an old photo.

writing.sentence: The music is too loud. Turn it ___.
I can't put up ___ the noise any longer.
Could you look ___ the dog this weekend?

writing.question: Rewrite formally: "They called the meeting off."
Rewrite in spoken English: "I cannot tolerate this noise."
Use "figure out" in a sentence about work.
Your car has broken down and you will be late. Write the message you send.

quiz.q: Which sentence fits a formal email best?
options: We called the whole thing off.
We had to knock it on the head.

quiz.q: "I can't put up with it" means ___.
She ___ the job offer because the salary was too low.
